terms.gloss: former, earlier, as it once was
evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.5b.2: tua prīstina dignitās et glōria (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 7.54: in prīstinum statum redīssent
terms.comment: Of a state, a habit or a standing one had before: in prīstinum statum redīre, to go back to how things were.

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 154: quī quondam in hostīs lēnissimus exīstimābātur, hōc tempore
Tib. 3.1.23: vir quondam, nunc frāter (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin has no adjective for a former husband or a former teacher; it says what he once was: vir quondam, “once a husband”, or with a clause, quī … fuit.

evidence: Cic. Har. Resp. 15: annō superiōre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of time before the present Cicero says superior (Lewis & Short, s.v. prior); see last (the one before this).

phrases.latin: hoc sī quis pretiī cupidus vīdisset tuī, ōlim redīssēs ad splendōrem prīstinum
phrases.english: if someone who knew your worth had seen you, you would long ago have gone back to your former splendour

phrases.latin: patre itaque meō rogante … ad prīstinam cōnsuētūdinem rediī
phrases.english: so, at my father’s request, … I went back to my former habit

phrases.latin: populum Rōmānum, quī quondam in hostīs lēnissimus exīstimābātur, hōc tempore domesticā crūdēlitāte labōrāre
phrases.english: that the Roman people, once thought the gentlest of nations even towards its enemies, now suffers from cruelty at home

pristinus.html: De Vaan 489, s.v. prior: from the zero grade *prīs- of the comparative, as in prīscus and prīdem.
